props.title: Gruber

sections.content: **Gruber (2010)** (2010) is a fascinating microbudget horror film that slipped under most viewers' radar. Made for just $15,000 by director Gary Cohen, it follows the psychological unraveling of a reclusive man who becomes obsessed with a mysterious entity he believes is stalking him. The film's claustrophobic atmosphere draws clear inspiration from Roman Polanski's Repulsion (1965) and The Tenant (1976), while its exploration of paranoia and isolation feels spiritually connected to **Pi** (1998) and Bug (2006).

sections.content: The film's strength lies in its minimalist approach, using a single location and limited cast to create maximum tension. Like Session 9 (2001) and Lake Mungo (2008), **Gruber** builds dread through suggestion rather than explicit scares. First-time actor James Westbrook delivers a remarkably committed performance as the titular character, carrying entire sequences alone on screen as his character's grip on reality becomes increasingly tenuous.

What sets **Gruber** apart from similar psychological horror films is its ambiguous treatment of mental illness. Unlike more exploitative takes like **Maniac** (1980) or **Henry: Portrait of a Serial Killer** (1986), Cohen's film maintains a compassionate view of its protagonist while never diminishing the horror of his situation. This approach aligns it more closely with sophisticated character studies like **Clean, Shaven** (1993). SUBHEAD: Technical Innovation on a Microbudget

sections.content: Despite severe financial constraints, **Gruber** achieves remarkable technical sophistication. Cohen's use of natural lighting and handheld camera work recalls the immediacy of **Blair Witch Project** (1999), while his sound design rivals more expensive productions like **Primer** (2004). The film demonstrates how creative limitations can spark innovation, much like **Following** (1998), Christopher Nolan's ultra-low-budget debut.
